```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)
set.seed(20250606)
```

Microsimulation (individual-level simulation) models track each patient
individually through health states, rather than tracking cohort proportions.
This enables patient-level heterogeneity, history-dependent transitions, and
individual event tracking --- features that cohort Markov models cannot
represent. This vignette explains microsimulation concepts, demonstrates how
to build a microsimulation model for ShinyCEA, and discusses practical
considerations for performance and reproducibility.

## Cohort vs. Microsimulation

| Feature | Cohort Markov | Microsimulation |
|:--------|:-------------|:----------------|
| Unit of analysis | Cohort proportions | Individual patients |
| Heterogeneity | Homogeneous cohort | Patient-level attributes (age, sex, risk) |
| Memory | Memoryless (Markov property) | Can depend on history (time in state, events) |
| Event tracking | Counts proportions | Counts per-patient events |
| Speed | Fast (matrix multiplication) | Slower (patient-level loops) |
| Variance | Deterministic | Stochastic (Monte Carlo noise) |
| When to use | Few states, homogeneous | Complex pathways, heterogeneity matters |

Microsimulation is recommended when the Markov assumption (memoryless
transitions) is violated --- for example, when the probability of death
increases with time spent in a disease state, or when treatment response
depends on individual patient characteristics (Krijkamp et al., 2018;
Brennan et al., 2006).

## The ShinyCEA Model Contract

ShinyCEA's model interface is agnostic to the simulation method. The
`simulate(pars, strategy)` function must return `list(cost, qaly)` ---
how you compute those values internally is entirely up to you. For
microsimulation, the function simulates N individual patients and returns
the **mean** cost and QALY across the cohort.

Optionally returning `trace` (a matrix of state proportions over time) and
`survival` (a data.frame with OS) enables the Survival and Traces tabs.

## Bundled Example: Chronic Disease Microsimulation

ShinyCEA includes a bundled microsimulation model with 4 states, heterogeneous
patient ages, age-dependent mortality, treatment-induced recovery, and
individual hospitalization events.

```{r load}
library(ShinyCEA)
model <- cea_microsim()
print(model)
```

### Model Structure

**States:**

1. **Stable** --- disease controlled, low cost, high utility
2. **Progressed** --- disease advancing, moderate cost
3. **Severe** --- high-cost state with hospitalization risk
4. **Dead** --- absorbing

**Strategies:**

- **Standard** --- baseline treatment (low drug cost, no recovery from progression)
- **New treatment** --- reduces progression risk (RR 0.60), reduces mortality
  (RR 0.75), enables recovery from Progressed back to Stable (3%/month),
  but costs more ($1,500 vs $200/month)

**Patient heterogeneity:**

Each patient gets an individual baseline age drawn from
$\text{Normal}(\mu = 45, \sigma = 10)$, which modifies mortality via an
age-dependent hazard ratio: $\text{HR}_{\text{age}} = 1.03^{\max(0, \text{age} - 45)}$.
This means older patients face progressively higher death rates.

**History-dependent features:**

- Hospitalization events are tracked per-patient per-cycle in the Severe
  state (Bernoulli draw with p = 0.15)
- Recovery from Progressed to Stable is only available under new treatment
  --- this is a treatment-specific transition that cohort models can
  represent but microsimulation tracks at the individual level

## Running the Model

### Deterministic Analysis

```{r deterministic}
# Use a smaller N for the vignette (faster)
params <- model$default_params()
params$base[params$name == "n_patients"] <- 500

det <- run_deterministic(model, params, wtp = 50000)
det$table[, c("Strategy", "Cost", "QALY", "NMB", "ICER_vsRef")]
```

Note: because microsimulation is stochastic, results will vary slightly
between runs. With N = 500, the Monte Carlo standard error is approximately
$\text{SE} \approx \text{SD}/\sqrt{500}$. Increase `n_patients` for more
precise estimates.

### Frontier Analysis

```{r frontier}
plot_frontier(det$frontier_status)
```

### Survival Curves

The `simulate()` function aggregates individual death times into a cohort
survival curve, enabling the Survival tab:

```{r survival}
surv_data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("standard", "new_treatment"), function(s) {
  res <- model$simulate(stats::setNames(as.list(params$base), params$name), s)
  df <- res$survival
  df$strategy <- s
  df
}))
plot_survival(surv_data, curve_name = "OS")
```

### State Traces

Individual state histories are aggregated into cohort-level proportions
per cycle:

```{r traces}
pars <- stats::setNames(as.list(params$base), params$name)
res <- model$simulate(pars, "new_treatment")

trace_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(res$trace), function(state) {
  data.frame(
    strategy = "new_treatment",
    time = seq(0, nrow(res$trace) - 1) / 12,
    state = state,
    prob = res$trace[, state]
  )
}))
plot_trace(trace_long, facet = FALSE)
```

### Tornado Diagram

One-way sensitivity analysis works the same as with cohort models --- each
parameter is varied while the microsimulation re-runs at each bound:

```{r tornado}
df_tor <- params[params$include_tornado &
                   (is.finite(params$lower) | is.finite(params$upper)), ]
tor <- build_tornado_data(df_tor, det$pars, model,
                          ref = "standard", target = "new_treatment",
                          metric = "INB", wtp = 50000)
if (nrow(tor) > 0) {
  plot_tornado(tor, base_val = unique(tor$base)[1],
               metric_label = "INB (new_treatment vs standard)")
}
```

## Building Your Own Microsimulation

### Step 1: Define the Simulation Loop

The core of a microsimulation is a per-patient, per-cycle loop. Here is
a minimal template:

```{r template, eval = FALSE}
simulate = function(pars, strategy) {
  N <- as.integer(pars[["n_patients"]])
  n_cycles <- as.integer(pars[["n_cycles"]])
  cl <- pars[["cycle_length"]]  # e.g., 1/12 for monthly

  # Patient attributes (heterogeneity)
  ages <- rnorm(N, mean = pars[["mean_age"]], sd = pars[["age_sd"]])

  # State vector: each patient starts in state 1

  state <- rep(1L, N)
  patient_cost <- numeric(N)
  patient_qaly <- numeric(N)

  for (t in seq_len(n_cycles)) {
    alive <- state < 4L  # state 4 = dead

    # Transition logic (vectorized across patients)
    u <- runif(N)
    # ... compute transition probabilities per patient ...
    # ... update state based on u < cumulative probabilities ...

    # Accumulate costs and QALYs for alive patients
    # ... based on current state ...
  }

  list(cost = mean(patient_cost), qaly = mean(patient_qaly))
}
```

### Step 2: Vectorize for Performance

The most common performance mistake is looping over patients in R:

```{r bad-loop, eval = FALSE}
# SLOW: nested loop over patients and cycles
for (i in 1:N) {
  for (t in 1:n_cycles) {
    # ... process patient i at cycle t ...
  }
}
```

Instead, vectorize across patients within each cycle:

```{r good-vectorized, eval = FALSE}
# FAST: vectorized across all patients per cycle
for (t in 1:n_cycles) {
  u <- runif(N)  # one draw per patient

  # Stable patients
  idx <- which(state == 1L)
  state[idx] <- ifelse(u[idx] < p_prog, 2L,
                 ifelse(u[idx] < p_prog + p_dead, 4L, 1L))

  # ... similarly for other states ...
}
```

This reduces a 1000-patient, 120-cycle simulation from minutes to
milliseconds.

### Step 3: Return Trace and Survival (Optional)

To enable the Survival and Traces tabs, aggregate individual trajectories:

```{r aggregate, eval = FALSE}
# Inside the cycle loop, after updating states:
trace[t + 1, ] <- c(
  mean(state == 1L),  # proportion in Stable
  mean(state == 2L),  # proportion in Progressed
  mean(state == 3L),  # proportion in Severe
  mean(state == 4L)   # proportion Dead
)

# After the loop:
os <- 1 - trace[, "Dead"]
survival <- data.frame(time = seq(0, n_cycles) * cl, surv = os, curve = "OS")

list(cost = mean(patient_cost), qaly = mean(patient_qaly),
     trace = trace, survival = survival)
```

### Step 4: Handle Reproducibility

Microsimulations are stochastic. For deterministic analysis (tornado,
threshold), you want reproducible results. Two approaches:

**Approach A: Fixed seed inside simulate() (simple but limits PSA)**

```{r seed-fixed, eval = FALSE}
simulate = function(pars, strategy) {
  set.seed(42)  # same results every call
  # ... microsim ...
}
```

**Approach B: Quasi-random patient attributes (recommended)**

Use quantile-based draws for patient heterogeneity, and `runif()` only
for transition events. The bundled example uses this approach for ages:

```{r quasi, eval = FALSE}
# Deterministic patient ages (no randomness)
ages <- mean_age + age_sd * qnorm((seq_len(N) - 0.5) / N)
```

This gives the same age distribution every time while allowing transition
randomness to vary across PSA iterations.

## PSA with Microsimulation

PSA adds an outer loop of parameter uncertainty on top of the inner
microsimulation. Each PSA iteration:

1. Draws parameter values from their distributions
2. Runs the microsimulation with those parameters
3. Records the mean cost and QALY

This is computationally expensive: 1,000 PSA iterations x 1,000 patients
= 1,000,000 individual simulations. Practical recommendations:

- **Reduce N for PSA**: Use N = 200--500 for PSA (the parameter uncertainty
  typically dominates the Monte Carlo noise)
- **Keep N large for deterministic**: Use N = 2,000--10,000 for the base case

```{r psa}
# Small N for PSA speed
psa_params <- model$default_params()
psa_params$base[psa_params$name == "n_patients"] <- 200

set.seed(20250606)
psa <- run_psa(model, psa_params, n_sim = 100)
cat("PSA: used =", psa$used, ", dropped =", psa$dropped, "\n")
```

```{r ceac}
ceac <- compute_ceac(psa$results, model$info()$strategies,
                     wtp_max = 100000, wtp_step = 5000)
plot_ceac(ceac)
```

## Performance Benchmarks

```{r benchmark}
params_bench <- model$default_params()
pars_bench <- stats::setNames(as.list(params_bench$base), params_bench$name)

for (n in c(200, 500, 1000, 2000)) {
  pars_bench[["n_patients"]] <- n
  t0 <- proc.time()
  model$simulate(pars_bench, "standard")
  elapsed <- (proc.time() - t0)[3]
  cat(sprintf("N = %5d: %.3f seconds\n", n, elapsed))
}
```

The vectorized implementation scales linearly with N. For interactive use
in ShinyCEA, N = 1,000 (the default) provides a good balance of precision
and responsiveness.

## Launching the App

```{r app, eval = FALSE}
# Launch with the microsimulation model
run_cea_app(cea_microsim())

# Or combine with cohort models for comparison
run_cea_app(cea_microsim(), cea_sick_sicker())
```

All ShinyCEA features work with microsimulation models:
deterministic analysis, tornado, two-way DSA, threshold analysis, PSA,
CEAC, expected loss, EVPI/EVPPI, scenarios, subgroups, BIA, weighted
comparators, and report generation.

## When to Use Microsimulation vs. Cohort Models

| Use cohort (Markov) when... | Use microsimulation when... |
|:---------------------------|:---------------------------|
| States are few (<10) | Many states or complex pathways |
| Transitions are memoryless | Transitions depend on history |
| Population is homogeneous | Patient heterogeneity matters |
| Speed is critical (PSA with many iterations) | Individual event tracking needed |
| Analytical tractability preferred | Competing risks with interactions |

Many decisions start with a cohort model for rapid iteration, then move
to microsimulation when heterogeneity or history-dependence is important
for the decision. ShinyCEA's model interface supports both without
changing any analysis code.
